bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: With every input rejected, any rejects with an AggregateError whose .errors array preserves each individual reason in input order — name, 2, and the second message. Nothing is lost, unlike race, which would have reported only mirror A.
hints: Total failure of any produces a special error type carrying ALL reasons.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions: Export `fastest(promises)` returning a promise of whichever input settles first (use Promise.race).
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: A thin wrapper, but naming it documents intent at call sites. The delayed-vs-immediate test shows settlement time (not array order) picking the winner.
hints: This one IS Promise.race.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions: Export async `firstFulfilled(promises)` returning the first FULFILLED value (Promise.any). If all reject, throw `new Error('none fulfilled')` instead of the AggregateError.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: any does the heavy lifting; the catch swaps its AggregateError for a domain-specific message — the rethrow-with-context pattern applied to a combinator. Callers see your API’s vocabulary, not the engine’s.
hints: await Promise.any in a try; translate the AggregateError in the catch.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions: Export `allOrNull(promises)` returning a promise of the array of ALL values — or `null` (not a rejection) if any input rejects.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: all’s fail-fast plus catch-to-null gives "complete set or nothing" as a plain value. When the pieces are only useful together (all config sections, all chunks), partial results are noise — null says so cleanly.
hints: Promise.all with one .catch on the end.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions: Export async `countFulfilled(promises)` returning HOW MANY inputs fulfilled (never rejecting).
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: Health dashboards in one line: "17 of 20 checks passing" is allSettled + filter + length. The combinator guarantees you wait for everyone before counting.
hints: allSettled, filter by status, length.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions: Export async `partitionSettled(promises)` returning `{ fulfilled: [values], rejected: [messages] }` — each list in input order.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: Identical in spirit to collectErrors from the last lesson with a different output shape — demonstrating that once outcomes are DATA, reshaping them is ordinary array work, no promise machinery required.
hints: The partition pattern over allSettled records.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions: Export async `settledValues(promises)` returning JUST the fulfilled values in input order, silently dropping rejections.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: Best-effort aggregation — show the search results that came back, skip the shards that timed out. Deliberately dropping errors is a policy decision; this helper makes it explicit and greppable instead of accidental.
hints: filter then map over the allSettled records.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions: Export `myRace(promises)` (non-empty array) reimplementing Promise.race with `new Promise`: settle with whichever input settles first, value or rejection. Do not use Promise.race.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: Three lines, powered entirely by settle-once: every input gets permission to settle the outer promise, and whichever calls resolve/reject first wins — all later calls are the documented no-ops from the promises lesson. The "weird" rule turns out to be the feature race is built on.
hints: Attach resolve as the success handler and reject as the failure handler of EVERY input — first caller wins.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions: Export async `anyOr(promises, fallback)` returning the first fulfilled value, or `fallback` when every input rejects (never rejecting).
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: any + catch-to-value composes "try every mirror" with "degrade gracefully" — the end state is always usable. Compare firstFulfilled (which re-throws): same mechanism, different failure policy; APIs are defined by these policy choices.
hints: Promise.any in a try; the catch returns the fallback.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions: Export async `rejectedReasons(promises)` returning the array of rejection Error MESSAGES in input order (fulfilled inputs contribute nothing). Use allSettled.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: Functionally this is AggregateError’s .errors list, but available even when SOME inputs succeeded — any only aggregates on total failure. Building it from allSettled shows the combinators are conveniences over one primitive: wait for everything, then inspect the records.
hints: allSettled; keep only rejected records; extract reason.message.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.instructions:
Export `myAll(promises)` reimplementing Promise.all with `new Promise` (do not use Promise.all/allSettled):
- fulfill with the array of values IN INPUT ORDER once every input fulfills
- reject with the first rejection reason
- `myAll([])` fulfills immediately with `[]`
- plain (non-promise) values in the array must work
bootforge/async-js/patterns/combinators/.explanation: The two classic bugs this design avoids: push() would order results by COMPLETION (results[i] = value pins them to input positions), and forgetting the empty-array case leaves the promise pending forever (zero pending inputs means nothing ever decrements the counter). The countdown-plus-index pattern generalizes to any "wait for N things" problem, and rejection handling again rides on settle-once: the first reject wins, later settles are no-ops.
hints: Store each value at its INDEX (results[i] = value), not with push — completion order lies.
Count down `remaining`; resolve when it hits zero. Handle the empty array before the loop.
Pass reject as the second .then argument — settle-once makes extra rejections harmless.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: What is the standard implementation of `delay(ms)`?
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: Passing resolve directly as the setTimeout callback is the whole trick: when the timer fires, the promise fulfills (with undefined). This is promisification at its smallest — and the base of every timing utility.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Why must retry take a FUNCTION `fn` rather than a promise?
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: retry(fetchUser(1), 3) starts ONE request and re-awaits its fixed outcome three times. retry(() => fetchUser(1), 3) can genuinely try again. The function-vs-promise distinction is the difference between a value and a recipe for producing one.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Why is `Promise.race` the right tool for a timeout wrapper?
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: The deadline promise rejects after ms; race mirrors the first settlement. Work faster than the deadline → its result; slower → the timeout rejection. Remember race cancels nothing — the slow work continues, you just stop waiting.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: What does `await delay(50)` evaluate to (with the standard implementation)?
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: setTimeout invokes resolve with no meaningful argument, so the promise fulfills with undefined. delay is used purely for its timing side effect; wrap it (delayValue) when you want a value to arrive late.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: When is a SEQUENTIAL mapper (one item at a time) the right choice over Promise.all?
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: Sequential processing trades speed for politeness and ordering guarantees. Rate limits, connection pools of one, and must-happen-in-order writes all demand it — which is why mapSeries sits beside mapAsync in utility libraries.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: 'zero' prints immediately — the chain is attached but dormant until the 5ms timer resolves delay's promise. Then the links fire in order as microtasks: 'first', 'second'. A delay at the head postpones the entire chain, which is exactly how polling loops pace themselves.
hints: The whole chain waits for the timer; then its links run as microtasks.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: main() logs 'one' synchronously, suspends on the delay, the caller logs 'two', and 10ms later the resumed function logs 'three'. delay() is just a promisified timer — all the event-loop rules apply to it unchanged.
hints: main runs until its first await, then the caller continues.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: Calling a() then b() starts BOTH timers in the same tick (no await between the calls), so they wait concurrently: 'started both' prints first, b's 5ms timer fires ('b done'), then a's 25ms timer ('a done'). Unawaited async calls are the fire-together pattern from the parallel lesson.
hints: Both functions start immediately; their delays run concurrently.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export `delay(ms)` returning a promise that fulfills (with `undefined`) after `ms` milliseconds.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: resolve IS the timer callback — no wrapper arrow needed. The second test flushes a microtask and confirms the promise is still pending: only the macrotask timer settles it, tying this utility back to the event-loop lesson.
hints: Pass resolve straight into setTimeout.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export `delayValue(v, ms)` returning a promise that fulfills with `v` after `ms` milliseconds.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: One captured value turns delay into a late-arriving constant — ideal for simulating slow APIs in tests and demos. Note the arrow wrapper: setTimeout(resolve(v), ms) would CALL resolve immediately (the store-vs-call bug from the functions course).
hints: Like delay, but resolve needs an argument now — wrap it in an arrow.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export `withTimeout(promise, ms)`: fulfill with the promise's value if it settles within `ms` milliseconds; otherwise reject with `new Error('timed out')`. Use Promise.race.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: The deadline must REJECT — resolving would make timeouts masquerade as successful results. Race hands you whichever settles first, and the third test confirms genuine fast failures are not relabeled as timeouts. This wrapper guards every network call in production code.
hints: Build a promise that REJECTS after ms, then race it against the work.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export `timeoutOr(promise, ms, fallback)`: fulfill with the promise's value if it arrives within `ms`; otherwise fulfill with `fallback` (never reject on timeout).
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: One word changed — resolve instead of reject — and the policy flips from "timeouts are errors" to "timeouts degrade to a default" (show cached data if the fresh fetch is slow). Hard and soft timeouts are the same race with different deadline promises.
hints: Same race as withTimeout, but the deadline RESOLVES with the fallback.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export async `retry(fn, attempts)`: call the async function `fn` up to `attempts` times, returning the first successful result. If every attempt rejects, throw the LAST error. `fn` must be called fresh for each attempt.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: The call-count assertions pin down the real contract: stop immediately on success, call exactly `attempts` times on total failure, surface the LAST error (the freshest diagnosis). Everything hinges on fn being a factory — each fn() mints a brand-new attempt.
hints: A counted loop: return inside try on success; remember the error and continue on failure; throw after the loop.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export async `mapSeries(items, fn)`: apply the async `fn` to each item STRICTLY one at a time (never overlapping), returning results in order. The tests detect overlap.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: mapAsync’s sequential twin: same signature, opposite concurrency contract, so the choice is explicit at the call site. The in-flight counter proving max concurrency 1 is the same deterministic instrumentation used throughout this module.
hints: The await-in-loop pattern — here it is the specification, not a mistake.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export async `runQueue(tasks)` — an array of async functions taking no arguments. Run them one at a time, in order, and return their results. A task is only STARTED after the previous one finished.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: The queue holds RECIPES (functions), so nothing runs until its turn — the same function-vs-promise distinction retry depends on. The second test shows why order matters: later tasks observe earlier tasks’ effects, which parallel execution could not guarantee.
hints: Loop and await task() — note the parentheses: tasks hold functions, not promises.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export async `pollUntil(check, maxTries)`: call the async `check` repeatedly (up to `maxTries` times) until it returns a truthy value, and return that value. If it stays falsy every time, return `null`.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: Polling is retry’s cousin: retry treats exceptions as "not yet", polling treats falsy values as "not yet". Real pollers insert a delay between checks (compose with delay!) — the tests here use a counter so the logic can be verified without waiting.
hints: Loop, await the check, return on truthy; null after the loop.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export `timeoutAll(promises, ms)`: apply a per-promise timeout (reject with `new Error('timed out')` as in withTimeout) to EVERY promise, then combine with Promise.allSettled — returning its records.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: Two utilities snap together: the per-promise race enforces the deadline, allSettled keeps one slow straggler from sinking the batch. Composing small async tools like this — rather than writing one bespoke mega-function — is the payoff of the whole course.
hints: map each promise through your withTimeout, then allSettled the lot.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: Export async `retryWithDelay(fn, attempts, ms)`: like retry, but WAIT `ms` milliseconds between attempts (no wait before the first attempt, none after the last failure). Return the first success; after all attempts fail, throw the last error. Tests use tiny delays.
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: Two utilities composed: the retry loop supplies the attempts, an awaited delay paces them. The `i > 0` guard encodes the real-world policy (first try immediately, pause only between retries) — note the third test would be slow if you delayed before attempt one. Production versions grow the delay each round (exponential backoff), a one-line change: `delay(ms * 2 ** (i - 1))`.
hints: Compose retry with delay: `if (i > 0) await delay(ms)` at the top of the loop.
Guarding with i > 0 keeps the first attempt instant.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions: This retry is broken: it calls `fn()` ONCE and then re-awaits the same settled promise on every "attempt", so it can never recover from a transient failure. Fix it to make a fresh call per attempt (keep the same exported signature).
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: The starter awaits the same rejected promise three times — and a settled promise replays its outcome forever, so attempts 2 and 3 are re-reading attempt 1’s failure. Moving fn() inside the try makes each iteration a genuine new attempt. The call-counting test is the giveaway instrument: the broken version shows calls === 1 no matter how many "retries" happen.
hints: How many times does fn actually RUN in the starter? Count the fn() calls.
Move the call inside the loop: await fn() per attempt.

bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.instructions:
Export async `mapLimit(items, limit, fn)`: apply async `fn` to every item with AT MOST `limit` calls in flight at once — a worker-pool, not batches: as soon as any call finishes, the next item starts.
Return results in input order. (A batch implementation also passes — the cap and order are what the tests enforce.)
bootforge/async-js/patterns/async-utilit.explanation: The worker-pool is the production-grade concurrency cap: unlike batches, a finished worker immediately pulls the next item, so slow items never stall unrelated work. The shared counter needs no locks because the claim is synchronous — single-threaded JavaScript’s quiet superpower. Index-addressed writes (results[i] = ...) reuse the ordering trick from myAll. This exact function ships in p-limit, async.mapLimit, and most scraper/importer codebases.
hints: Spawn `limit` workers; each worker loops: claim the next index, process it, repeat until none remain.
A shared `next` counter is safe — JS is single-threaded, and the claim (read + increment) happens synchronously between awaits.
Write results[i] by claimed index to keep input order.
